FREEDOM OF EXPRESSION — freedom of speech and the right to freely express opinion on any subject — FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS — balance between freedom of expression and other fundamental freedoms —
CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS
—
s. 1

Oakes

HUMAN RIGHTS — nature and purpose of human rights legislation — EXEMPTIONS — human rights legislation — DISCRIMINATION —
bona fide
justification — INTERPRETATION OF STATUTES — definition of "caused to be published", "contempt", "hatred", "likely to expose" and "opinion"

PARTIES — name of director of respondent company named as individual respondent — director of respondent company named as respondent

Summary:
The Alberta Court of Queen's Bench answered five questions of law referred to it by a Human Rights Panel. The Panel was appointed to hear a complaint against Alberta Report alleging that it had breached
s. 2
of the
Alberta Human Rights, Citizenship and Multiculturalism Act
by publishing an article that exposed Jewish persons to hatred or contempt.

Section 2(1) provides that "no person shall publish or display or caused to be published... or displayed any statement, publication, notice, sign, symbol, or other representation that (a) indicates discrimination or an intention to discriminate”¦or (b) is likely to expose a person or a class of persons to hatred or contempt because of the[ir] race [or] religious beliefs..."

Section 2(2) provides that: "Nothing in this section shall be deemed to interfere with the free expression of opinion on any subject". Also, s. 2(b) of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
guarantees that everyone has the fundamental freedoms of thought, belief, opinion and expression.

The Panel posed these questions to the Court:

1. Is the fact that an individual holds a position on the Board of Directors or as an officer of an entity that is alleged to have breached s. 2(1) of the Act sufficient reason to name that individual as a respondent to the complaint?

2. Is it necessary for a statement, publication, or notice to be phrased, designed or structured in a particular way in order to constitute an "opinion" within the meaning of s. 2(2)?

3. Does s. 2(2) bar the Panel from finding a breach of s. 2(1) when the respondent can establish that he or she is freely expressing his or her opinion?

4. If s. 2(2) is not a bar, can s. 2(2) be used after a finding of a breach of s. 2(1) to justify that breach?

5. What standards must the Panel apply to determine whether a representation "is likely to expose a person to hatred or contempt"?

To the first question the Court answered that a person may be named as a respondent where there is prima facie evidence on the face of the complaint, or from investigation, which demonstrates that he or she is causally connected, directly or indirectly, to the publication or display of the disputed material. It will be a question of fact in each case.

The Court also determined that there is no particular way a statement or notice needs to be designed or structured in order to constitute an "opinion" under s. 2(2). It is the content of the message, and the context in which it is delivered, which will determine whether it is an "opinion".

Regarding the interaction between ss. 2(1) and 2(2), the Court reasoned that s. 2(2) provides neither a defence nor a justification for a breach of s. 2(1). If s. 2(2) were interpreted as an absolute defence to a violation of s. 2(1), as Alberta Report contended it was, that would render s. 2(1) hollow. A respondent would merely have to establish that his or her expression was opinion in order to avoid the complaint. Excluding opinions from the reach of s. 2(1) would go a long way towards defeating the purpose of the legislation. Additionally, accepting that s. 2(2) provides an absolute defence to a breach of s. 2(1) would mean accepting the proposition that freedom of expression as guaranteed in
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
overrides the protected interests in freedom of religion and equality. Such a conclusion would be contrary to the established interpretive principle that one Charter right cannot trump another.

The Court also reasoned that s. 2(2) does not provide a defence or justification for a breach of s. 2(1), because defences are found in other sections of the Act. Specifically, s. 2(3) permits the use of symbols to identify facilities customarily used by one gender, or the display or publication by non-profit groups of statements indicating a membership qualification for their organizations. Section 11.1 states that an alleged contravention will be deemed not to have occurred if it was reasonable and justifiable in the circumstances.

Rather than a defence, the Court found that s. 2(2) is an admonition to balance the two competing objectives of freedom of expression and the eradication of discrimination. A two-step process is required by the Act. Once a prima facie breach is found, the Panel must go on to specifically balance freedom of expression against the particular violation.

The standards which must be applied when determining whether a statement is "likely to expose a person or group to hatred or contempt" have been settled by a majority of the Supreme Court of Canada in Canada (Human Rights Comm.) v. Taylor. Different considerations apply to each term. Consideration of whether a particular communication is "likely to expose" a group to hatred or contempt should focus on the impact on the group. Any analysis must be highly contextual, and should consider the content and tone of the message, the credibility and context of the publication, and the vulnerability of the target group.

I.  INTRODUCTION

[
1
]  This special case, pursuant to
s. 27
of the
Alberta
Human Rights, Citizenship and Multiculturalism Act,

R.S.A. 1980, c. H-11
.7 (the "
Act
"), arises from questions of law (enumerated below) submitted to the Court for an opinion by the Alberta Human Rights and Citizenship Commission Panel (the "Panel") hearing the complaint in this case.

II.  FACTS

[
2
]
Alberta Report,
now the
Report Newsmagazine,
is a magazine published by United Western Communications Ltd. The October 31, 1997, edition of
Alberta Report
contained an article headlined "A Canmore Mall Project Ends in a Bitter Feud" (the "Article"). The Article summarized a dispute between an American promoter, Benson Flanzbaum, and a Canadian builder, Fred Schickedanz, relating to a failed property development in Canmore. The Article noted that Mr. Flanzbaum owned a company called Canmore Development Corp. that had arranged to purchase land for the project from another company called Oshawa Holdings Ltd. The Article described Mr. Flanzbaum's appearance as follows:

A profuse collection of rings adorns Mr. Flanzbaum's fingers, and his open shirts display more golden jewellery on a hirsute chest.

The final sentence in the Article reads:

One professional planner comments on the failed project: "North American commercial real estate is dominated by firms that often happen to be Jewish owned [e.g. Oshawa and Canmore Development]. The retail sector is much the same. Like cliques everywhere, some of these people tend to deal with each other, and Mr. Schickedanz is an outsider."

[
3
]  On May 4, 1998, the Jewish Defence League of Canada (the "League") and its Executive Director, Harvey Kane, filed a complaint alleging that the Article contravened s. 2 of the
Act.
The complaint made particular mention of the two portions of the Article set out above.

[
4
]  The complaint named
Alberta Report,
Link Byfield, Michael Byfield and Ted Byfield as respondents. Michael Byfield wrote the Article. Link Byfield was
Alberta Report
's editor and publisher and reviewed the Article before printing it. Ted Byfield founded
Alberta Report
and sat on the Board of Directors but was neither author, editor nor publisher of the Article. Together these individuals will be referred to as "the Byfields". All of the respondents shall be collectively referred to as the "
Alberta Report
".

[
5
]  On May 27, 1998,
Alberta Report
responded to the complaint by denying a breach of the
Act,
and by raising s. 2(2) of the
Act
as a defence.

[
6
]  The Commission's efforts to settle the complaint through conciliation were unsuccessful and on August 13, 1999, the Commission dismissed the complaint.

[
7
]  The League and Mr. Kane appealed the dismissal of the complaint. The Chief Commissioner reviewed the dismissal and appointed the Panel to deal with the complaint.

[
8
]  Several questions of law have arisen in the course of the proceedings before the Panel. The Panel adjourned its May 2000 hearing to apply to the Court of Queen's Bench for its opinion on these questions.

[
9
]  In addition to the Director of the Alberta Human Rights Commission, Mr. Kane, the League and the
Alberta Report,
a number of interveners were granted leave to participate in the hearing of this matter. Specifically, submissions were made on an intervener basis by the Legal Education and Action Fund ("LEAF"), the Alberta Association of Community Living ("AACL"), the Calgary Herald and Mr. Lawrence Oshanek. Pursuant to a time-limited invitation extended by the Court, all of the parties and interveners, with the exception of Mr. Kane and the League, submitted written submissions for the Court's consideration. The Panel is a neutral party in this matter and has not made any submissions in relation to the questions which it has put before the Court.

III.  QUESTIONS OF LAW

[
10
]  The Panel requests the opinion of this Court on the following questions of law:

1.    Is the fact that an individual holds either a position on the Board of Directors or as an officer of an entity that is alleged to have breached s. 2(1) of the
Act
sufficient reason to name that individual as a respondent to the complaint? If it is sufficient reason to name the individual, would any finding of liability be based on the individual having "caused" the offending materials to be published, issued or displayed?

2.    Is it necessary for a statement, publication, notice, sign, symbol, emblem or other representation to be phrased, designed or structured in any particular way in order to constitute an "opinion" within the meaning of s. 2(2) of the
Act
?

3.    Can a breach of s. 2(1) of the
Act
be found in the face of a defence based on s. 2(2) of the
Act?
That is, does s. 2(2) of the
Act
bar the Panel from finding a breach of s. 2(1) of the
Act
when the alleged wrongdoer can establish that he/she is freely expressing his/her opinion?

4.    If s. 2(2) of the
Act
is not a bar to finding a breach of s. 2(1) of the
Act
, can s. 2(2) be used after a finding of breach of s. 2(1) in order to justify that breach?

5.    What standards must the Panel apply to determine whether a representation "is likely to expose a person or a class of persons to hatred or contempt"? Are different considerations applied to questions of "contempt" as opposed to questions of "hatred"?

IV.  STATUTORY AND CHARTER PROVISIONS

[
11
]  Subsections 2(1) and (2) of the
Act
read:

2(1)    No person shall publish, issue or display or cause to be published, issued or displayed before the public any statement, publication, notice, sign, symbol, emblem or other representation that

(a)   indicates discrimination or an intention to discriminate against a person or a class of persons, or

(b)   is likely to expose a person or a class of persons to hatred or contempt

because of the race, religious beliefs, colour, gender, physical disability, mental disability, age, ancestry, place of origin, marital status, source of income or family status of that person or class of persons.

(2)   Nothing in this section shall be deemed to interfere with the free expression of opinion on any subject.

[
12
]
Subsection 2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
,
R.S.C. 1985, Appendix II, No. 44, states:

2.       Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(b)   freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of the press and other media of communication;

[
13
]
Subsection 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
provides that:

52(1)   The Constitution of Canada is the supreme law of Canada, and any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency, of no force or effect.

V.  PARTIES' POSITIONS AND ANALYSIS

[
14
]  Given the number of parties involved and the various positions that they take in relation to each of the five questions before me, I have, for the sake of clarity, summarized each party's position separately in relation to each of the questions. I have not summarized Mr. Oshanek's position separately as the relevant portions of his submissions have been subsumed in the outline of the other parties' submissions and have, thus, been addressed. Moreover, as noted, Mr. Kane and the League made no timely submissions.

[
15
]  I should also note that there appeared to be some misunderstanding as to whether the questions posed related to only s. 2(1)(b), or to both s. 2(1)(a) and (b). As s. 2(1)(a) was not explicitly excluded I have included a consideration of that subsection where appropriate. However, some of the questions by their very nature were confined to an analysis of s. 2(1)(b).

1.    Is the fact that an individual holds either a position on the Board of Directors or as an officer of an entity that is alleged to have breached section 2(1) of the Act sufficient reason to name that individual as a respondent to the complaint? If it is sufficient reason to name the individual, would any finding of liability be based on the individual having "caused" the offending materials to be published, issued or displayed?

(a)  Positions of the Parties

THE DIRECTOR

[
16
]  The Director argues that, where a complaint is made against a publication in a newspaper, both the author of the representation (using the terminology of the
Act
) and the owner of the medium involved are properly named as respondents. It suggests that generally a member of a Board could also be named where that member holds another position such as editor or publisher, such that the member actively "caused" the offending materials to be published, issued or displayed.

[
17
]  Additionally, the Director submits that, in some circumstances, it will be necessary to pierce the corporate veil and name a board member as a respondent despite the fact that that member did not directly "cause" the publication. It suggests that piercing the corporate veil in this manner would be appropriate where the directors, though not directly involved in causing the publication, are responsible for instigating the impugned behaviour. This, the Director submits, would prevent individuals from setting up corporations to shield themselves from the consequences of breaching the
Act
and would ensure that any remedial measures ordered by the Panel were realized. The Director acknowledges that this would require an expansive definition of "cause to be published" and suggests this is consistent with the interpretation of the
Act
as remedial.

[
18
]  The Director envisages that such individuals would be named in a complaint where there is
prima facie
evidence, on the face of the complaint, indicating that they ought to be so named. The Panel would then investigate and determine, on a balance of probabilities, whether there is any evidence to support the allegations. Where such evidence exists, the individuals would remain named in the complaint.

ALBERTA REPORT

[
19
]
Alberta Report
submits that the purpose of human rights legislation is not to punish wrongdoing or wrongdoers, but to prevent discrimination and provide limited compensation. Thus, the
Act
should not be interpreted to allow for the potential liability of directors and officers who are not causally connected to the publication, issuance or display of the offensive representation. Otherwise, those who are not causally connected would be unfairly labelled and stigmatized. It is the conduct of the individual in question, rather than their position, that is determinative of whether they should be named as a respondent. If a director or officer was potentially liable solely as a result of his/her acquiescence, knowledge or assent, one would expect to see language to that effect in the
Act.

[
20
]
Alberta Report
argues that where the complaint involves the actual publication or issuance of an allegedly offensive representation, only the publishing company is properly a respondent, as that would be the "person" that has actually published the representation. It submits that a director or officer should not be named as a respondent unless it is objectively evident, either when the complaint is filed or through an investigation of a complaint, that a particular director or officer directly "caused" the publication, issuance, or display of an impugned representation. In oral argument, the
Alberta Report
suggested that if it were not objectively evident on the face of the complaint that the individuals ought to be named as respondents, then the corporation should be named first and individuals would only be added after an investigation determined that they were causally connected to the alleged breach.

[
21
]  Finally, the
Alberta Report
takes the position that there are two possible interpretations of when it would be appropriate for an individual, including a director or officer, to be named as the person having "caused". the publication: where that individual is the publisher or the editor. The
Alberta Report
submits that if the category of potential respondents is not limited in this fashion, it will lead to an abuse of the complaints process.

LEAF

[
22
]  LEAF takes no position on this issue.

CALGARY HERALD

[
23
]  The
Calgary Herald
submits that s. 2(1) of the
Act
appears to create a strict liability offence. In order to prove wrongdoing, the Panel must find that a person committed the act of publishing, issuing or displaying the allegedly offensive material. The
Act
does not create vicarious liability for persons because they are an owner, shareholder or director of the publishing corporation. Only those who created the representation or had sufficient operational control over the content of the publication can be said to have committed the impugned act of placing the representation before the public.

[
24
]  The
Calgary Herald
also argues that s. 2(1) of the
Act
should not be interpreted to impose liability on a publisher for printing the statements of a third party solely for the purpose of reporting news. This, it suggests, could not be justified as a reasonable limitation on freedom of expression and freedom of the press under
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
.

AACL

[
25
]  The AACL takes no position on this issue.

(b)  Analysis

[
26
]  As will be apparent from the summary of the parties' positions, there was not a great deal of disagreement in relation to this question. All who made submissions agreed that some degree of causation was necessary before an individual director or officer should be named in the complaint. I agree with that assessment.

[
27
]  The
Act
does not impose vicarious liability. Thus, on a plain reading of s. 2(1), a board member or an officer of an entity should only be named as a respondent to a complaint if he or she published, issued or displayed or caused to be issued, published or displayed, any of the prohibited material.

[
28
]  The proper focus of s. 2(1) is on the conduct of the person alleged to have breached the
Act,
not the status or position of that person. If the intention of the section was to extend liability to officers and directors of a company making a representation on the basis of their having knowledge of or having acquiesced in the act or omission of the company resulting in the publication, issuance or display, one would expect to see language to that effect in s. 2(1). The omission of such language is particularly telling when one considers that the Legislature has used specific language to extend liability on that basis in other
Acts
– see: ss. 114(1) and 218 of the
Business Corporations Act,
R.S.A. 1980, c. B-15, s. 168(1) of the
Securities Act,
S.A. 1981, c. S-6.1 and
s. 165(1)
of the
Fair Trading Act,
S.A. 1998, c. F-1.05 for example.

[
29
]  My conclusion in this regard is fortified by the fact that the purpose of human rights legislation is to prevent and compensate for discrimination, rather than punish the wrongdoers. The Supreme Court of Canada emphasized this purpose in the context of the
Canadian Human Rights Act,
R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6, in
Canadian National Railway Co.
v.
Canada (Human Rights Commission) and Action travail des femmes,

1987 CanLII 109 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R. 1114
,
40 D.L.R. (4
th
) 193
at 206
[8 C.H.R.R. D/4210 at D/4224, § 33239], where Dickson C.J.C. states:

The purposes of the
Act
would appear to be patently obvious, in light of the powerful language of
s. 2
. In order to promote the goal of equal opportunity for each individual to achieve "the life that he or she is able and wishes to have", the Act seeks to prevent all "discriminatory practices" based,
inter alia,
on sex. It is the practice itself which is sought to be precluded. The purpose of the Act is not to punish wrongdoing but to prevent discrimination.

The last point is an important one and it deserves to be underscored. There is no indication that the purpose of the
Canadian Human Rights Act
is to assign or to punish moral blameworthiness.

[
30
]  Dickson C.J.C. reiterated this purpose
in
Canada (Human Rights Comm.)
v.
Taylor
,

1990 CanLII 26 (SCC)
,
[1990] 3 S.C.R. 892
at 917
[13 C.H.R.R. D/435 at D/448, § 36]:

The aim of human rights legislation ... is not to bring the full force of the state's power against a blameworthy individual for the purpose of imposing punishment.

and at 933 [D/459, § 69]:

... the purpose and impact of human rights codes is to prevent discriminatory effects rather than to stigmatize and punish those who discriminate.

[
31
]  Because the intention of the
Act
is remedial and preventative, s. 2(1) should be interpreted to allow for the potential liability of only those directors or officers who are causally connected with the publication, issuance, or display, of an offending representation.

[
32
]  "Cause to be published" for the purposes of s. 2(1) must be given a broad interpretation. In other words, a respondent does not need to be involved in the publication, issuance or display of the representation in a "hands on" sense to be liable under the
Act.
It will be sufficient, in my view, for a director, officer or board member to be indirectly involved. Indirect involvement which may expose an individual to liability may include instigating or promoting the publication, issuance or display. The degree of indirect involvement that will ground liability will have to be considered on a case-by-case basis as part of a full contextual review. This is consistent with the principle that human rights legislation should be given full effect through a "fair, large and liberal interpretation" (
Taylor
at 927 [D/455, § 58]).

[
33
]
Alberta Report
submits firstly that, in terms of print media, only the publishing corporation ought to be exposed to liability. If individuals are ever appropriately named as respondents it suggests the category of potential respondents ought to be limited to the publisher and/or the editor. It bases this submission on the fact that those are the individuals who generally have direct causal control over the publication. It argues further that a reporter, the author of an impugned representation, would not be a proper respondent and it cites
R.
v.
Dimmock,

[1999] N.B.J. No. 184 (QL)
(Q.B.)
in support of that proposition.

[
34
]  In
Dimmock
a number of reporters were charged with breaching the New Brunswick
Family Services Act
, S.N.B. 1983, c. F-2.2, by "causing to be published" the name of a child involved in a proceeding before the Court. On appeal, the Court of Queen's Bench affirmed the not guilty verdict on the basis that it was the editors or publisher, not the reporters, who "caused" the articles to be published.

[
35
]  The remedial nature of the
Act
dictates against limiting the pool of potential respondents to the publishing corporations. If corporate entities were the appropriate respondents, any remedial order ultimately made by a Panel may be of little effect as it would permit the individual(s) responsible to shield themselves behind a corporation. Obviously, this would do little to advance the purpose of the
Act.

[
36
]  Nor am I prepared to limit potential respondents to a complaint, where media is involved, on the basis of the particular position an individual may hold. Creating limitations as to who can be named as respondents without the benefit of specific fact situations would not allow for a proper consideration of the context in any particular case. In other words, to say that only publishers can be named as respondents in complaints involving print media, may allow any individuals who are not publishers and who are "causing the publication", to avoid the
Act.
It is the conduct of the particular individual that will determine if they are an appropriate respondent in a given case. (I have used "individual" here to distinguish from a corporation, although both would be included in "person" under s. 2(1).)

[
37
]  I acknowledge that in
Dimmock
the New Brunswick Court of Queen's Bench held that it was editors or publishers who "caused" the articles. However, that case was concerned with a breach of the
New Brunswick
Family Services Act,

[
66

[

[

Calgary Herald

Freedom of the press is not a separate right, but is subsumed within freedom of expression. Nonetheless, as noted in
CJC,
the express mention of freedom of the press in s. 2(b) indicates that it is a fundamental value in our society.

[
93
]  While I acknowledge the importance of free press to a democratic society, I am also of the view that this freedom must be exercised responsibly, particularly in light of the enormous influence that the media enjoys. It is, therefore, crucial that limits and counterbalances such as s. 2(2) apply to the media. Exempting the media from the
Act
in this regard would be tantamount to presuming that the media is always neutral in its reporting. I am not prepared to make that presumption.

[
94
]  In every case, including those in which members of the media are named as respondents, it will be incumbent upon the Panel to look carefully at all of the circumstances. In those cases where the media is named as a respondent, the Panel's consideration will generally entail a review of how the article was reported. This might include factors such as: the tone of the article; whether both or only one side of an event was reported; and whether there was any editorial or commentary surrounding the statement, and, if so, whether it was disapproving or supportive. This list is not exhaustive. Many things will determine whether a reported statement is discriminatory. The media must remain responsible for how they report what may be sensitive subject matter.

[
95
]  The
Calgary Herald
suggests that only "mainstream" media should be given an automatic exemption from the reach of s. 2(1) of the

In addition to the reasons cited above, which apply to all media reporting, there is no workable definition of "mainstream". Further, as was demonstrated in
CJC,
the press, including "mainstream" media, has in the past played a role in reinforcing attitudes of discrimination. The impact of such irresponsible reporting is arguably more damaging when it is distributed by "mainstream" media as it may serve to bolster the credibility of the statement and widen its circulation.

[
96
]  Finally, the press is not without a defence in circumstances where it has been named as a respondent to a complaint as a result of having reported a statement which in and of itself is a violation of the
Act.
In that event, the respondent may rely on s. 11.1 to justify its actions.

(c)  Opinion

[
97
]  Section 2(2) is an admonition to balance freedom of expression and the eradication of discrimination in the consideration of a complaint under s. 2 of the
Act.
That section is neither a defence nor a justification for a breach of s. 2(1). Justifications and defences to a breach of s. 2(1) are found at s. 2(3) and s. 11 of the
Act.
Balancing the eradication of discrimination and freedom of expression will occur indirectly in the consideration of a complaint under s. 2(1)(b). In relation to both s. 2(1)(a) and s. 2(1)(b), a direct balancing of these interests will occur after a
prima facie
breach of either of those sections is found.

5.    What standards must the Panel apply to determine whether a representation "is likely to expose a person or a class of persons to hatred or contempt". Are different considerations applied to questions of "contempt" as opposed to questions of "hatred"?

(a)  Positions of the Parties

[
98
]  The Director submits that "likely to expose" and "hatred" and "contempt" should be interpreted pursuant to
the principles set out in
Nealy
v.
Johnston

1989 CanLII 151 (CHRT)
,
10 C.H.R.R. D/6450 (C.H.R.T.)
,
Taylor
and

]

argues that

]  In applying the appropriate standard, LEAF argues that the Panel should have regard to evidence from the community, including members of the target group, as well as expert evidence. [

]  The

.

(b)  Analysis

[
104
]  Questions 3 and 4 considered the interplay between s. 2(1) and s. 2(2). Question 5 involves an analysis of how s. 2(1)(b) ought to be applied. In other words, how or by what standards will a representation be determined to be likely to expose a person or group of persons to hatred and contempt?

[
105
]  As a result of the various definitions and tests which have evolved in relation to the standard to be applied in a determination of whether legislation in the nature of s. 2(1) has been breached, I propose to divide this question into sub-issues. Accordingly, I will deal first with the definitions of "hatred" and "contempt" and then discuss the meaning of "likely to expose". Thereafter, I will discuss the tests that have developed in applying these standards.

(I)  "HATRED" AND "CONTEMPT"

[
106
]  The Tribunal
in
Nealy
,
at D/6469, defined the terms "hatred" and "contempt". That definition was
approved by the Supreme Court in
Taylor
,
where Dickson C.J.C. states, at 927 [D/455, § 59, quoting
Nealy
]:

In defining "hatred" the Tribunal [
in
Taylor
] applied the definition in the
Oxford English Dictionary
(1971 ed.) which reads:

active dislike, detestation, enmity, ill-will, malevolence.

The Tribunal drew on the same source for their definition of contempt [at p. 28]. It was characterized as

the condition of being condemned or despised; dishonour or disgrace.

As there is no definition of "hatred" or "contempt" within the [
Canadian Human Rights Act
] it is necessary to rely on what might be described as common understandings of the meaning of these terms. Clearly these are terms which have a potentially emotive content and how they are related to particular factual contexts by different individuals will vary. There is nevertheless an important core of meaning in both, which the dictionary definitions capture.
With "hatred" the focus is a set of emotions and feelings which involve extreme ill will towards another person or group of persons. To say that one "hates" another means in effect that one finds no redeeming qualities in the latter.
It is a term, however, which does not necessarily involve the mental process of "looking down" on another or others. It is quite possible to "hate" someone who one feels is superior to one in intelligence, wealth or power.
None of the synonyms used in the dictionary definition for "hatred" give any clues to the motivation for the ill will. "Contempt" is by contrast a term which suggests a mental process of "looking down" upon or treating as inferior the object of one's feelings. This is captured by the dictionary definition relied on
in
Taylor
... in the use of the terms "despised", "dishonour" or "disgrace". Although the person can be "hated" (i.e. actively disliked) and treated with "contempt" (i.e. looked down upon), the terms are not fully coextensive, because "hatred" is in some instances the product of envy of superior qualities, which "contempt" by definition cannot be.
[Emphasis added
in
Taylor
.
]

[
107
]  Accordingly, the definitions of "hatred" and "contempt", as those terms are used in human rights legislation, have been settled. As those definitions ascribe different meanings to the two terms, it will be necessary to apply different considerations to a determination of whether "hatred" or "contempt" has been established for the purposes of s. 2(1).

(II)  "LIKELY TO EXPOSE"

[
108
]  As noted in
CJC,
the meaning of "likely to expose" was not discussed explicitly by either the minority or the majority of the Court
in
Taylor
.

[
109
]  The Tribunal
in
Nealy
discussed the meaning of "expose", at D/6470 [§ 45656], and quoted with approval from the Tribunal's
decision in
Taylor
:

"Expose" is an unusual word to find in legislation designed to control hate propaganda. More frequently, as in the
Broadcasting Act Regulations, Post Office Act
provisions and in the various related sections of the
Criminal Code
,
the reference is to matter which is abusive or offensive, or to statements which serve to incite or promote hatred.

"Incite" means to stir up; "promote" means to support actively. "Expose" is a more passive word, which seems to indicate that an active effort or intent on the part of the communicator or a violent reaction on the part of the recipient are not envisaged. To expose to hatred also indicates a more subtle and indirect type of communication than vulgar abuse or overtly offensive language. "Expose" means: to leave a person unprotected; to leave without shelter or defence; to lay open (to danger, ridicule, censure etc.). In other words, if one is creating the right conditions for hatred to flourish, leaving the identifiable group open or vulnerable to ill-feelings or hostility, if one is putting them at risk of being hated, in a situation where hatred or contempt are inevitable, one then falls within the compass of s. 13(1) of the
Human Rights Act.

[
110
]  The
Nealy
Tribunal went on to consider the phrase "likely to expose" a person or persons to hatred or contempt and stated, at D/6470 [D/45657]:

... We note, as the excerpt suggests, that there is no need for the complainants to prove an active effort or intent on the part of the respondents to produce the adverse consequence contemplated by the section. Moreover, the use of the wording "likely to expose a person or persons to hatred or contempt" means that it is not necessary that evidence be adduced that any particular individual or group took the messages seriously and in fact directed hatred or contempt against another or others, still less that anyone has in fact been victimized in this way. It is enough to prove that the matter in the messages is more likely than not
to spark a positive reaction amongst some of the listeners to it which will likely in turn manifest itself in "hatred" or "contempt" towards the targets of the messages
. [Emphasis added.]

[
111
]
Nealy
applied
a standard of the "gullible or malevolent listener" to the potential impact of the communication. In
CJC,
the Panel rejected that standard. It found that, in light of the broader reach of the legislation at issue in that case (the prohibition of the issuance, publication or display of prohibited material), the application of
the standard set forth in
Nealy
would exceed the justifiable limits on freedom of expression.

[
112
]  Conversely, the Panel in
CJC
found that a "reasonable person" standard would be too onerous. It reasoned that this would be the case because "we generally believe that reasonable people will reject hate" [at D/27, § 127].

[
113
]  Instead of applying a new standard, the Panel in
CJC
recast the issue. It concluded that the issue was not about persuading a recipient to feel hatred or contempt, but about whether the effect of the communication was to increase the likelihood that members of a target group will be exposed to hatred or contempt.

[
114
]  The form or method of prohibited communication in the
Act
also includes publication, issuance or display of prohibited material. I agree with the decision in
CJC
that this casts a much wider net than was
the case in
Nealy
and thereby poses a greater threat to freedom of expression, particularly if combined with the "gullible or malevolent" thinker standard.

[
115
]  I do not, however, agree with the Tribunal in
CJC
that the issue turns on whether the message is "likely to increase the risk of exposure". I will discuss my conclusion in this regard more fully in the next section of this opinion. I do, however, agree with
CJC
that the test is not whether the communication is likely to persuade a recipient to feel hatred or contempt but rather the impact of the message on the target group. Accordingly, the inquiry ought to be whether it is more likely than not that the members of the target group will be exposed to hatred or contempt because the message makes it more acceptable for recipients to act on their feelings of hatred and contempt. This assessment would be made on a reasonable person standard. Thus, a communication will be "likely to expose" a person or group to hatred or contempt where it can be demonstrated that the reasonable listener would believe that the communication would make it more likely than not that the target group would be so exposed.

(III)  THE TESTS

[
116
]  In addition to the definitions which have developed, two tests have emerged to aid in the determination of whether a message is likely to expose a person or class of persons to hatred or contempt. One is a unitary test used in the Federal jurisdiction and the other is a two-part test which has been applied in British Columbia.

The Two-Part Test

[
117
]  On the basis of the definitions adopted
in
Nealy
and its own redefinition of the issues, the Tribunal in
CJC
prescribed a two-part test to be applied in considering whether a breach of s. 7(1)(b) of the 1996
British Columbia
Human Rights Code,
had occurred [at D/28, § 130]:

First, does the communication itself express hatred or contempt of a person or group on a basis of one or more of the listed grounds? Would a reasonable person understand this message as expressing hatred or contempt?

Second, assessed in its context, is the likely effect of the communication to make it more acceptable to others to manifest hatred or contempt against the person or group concerned? Would a reasonable person consider it likely to increase the risk of exposure of target group members to hatred or contempt?

[
118
]
In
Abrams
,
the Tribunal determined that the test set out in
CJC
was not a rigid test that was subject to mechanical application, but was one of many useful, analytical frameworks permitting a consideration of both the content and the effect of a message.

[
119
]  The Tribunal
in
Abrams
,
at § 59 [D/444], however, held that context played a more important role in the first arm of the test than allowed for by the
CJC
test. On that basis it restated the first arm test [at D/445, § 65]:

Would a reasonable person, informed about the context, understand the message as expressing hatred or contempt?

[
120
]
I agree with the Tribunal in
Abrams
that the tests developed in the jurisprudence must not be applied rigidly, particularly given that any standard applied will have to be responsive to the particular legislation at issue. I agree further that context plays a significant role in the entire consideration of whether there has been a breach of legislation designed to prohibit hatred and contempt. In referencing
Abrams,
I acknowledge that that decision has been referred back to the Tribunal for a consideration of the constitutional issues.

[
121
]  In my view, the question posed by the second arm of the test set out in
CJC,
would not yield a response which would satisfy our legislation. In other words, s. 2(1)(b) concerns itself with whether the message is "likely to expose", not whether the message is "likely to increase the risk of exposure". There is a substantive difference between these enquiries. Specifically, the
CJC
test focuses on risk, while the
Act
focuses on exposure.

[
122
]  Additionally, the phrase "likely to expose" is a balance of probabilities test. In other words, what s. 2(1)(b) seeks to prevent is representations which are more likely than not to expose a person or class of persons to hatred or contempt on the basis of the prohibited grounds. The test proposed in
CJC
would admit of a breach where there is a 1 percent chance of being exposed to hatred or contempt which is increased by 0.01 percent. This would effectively allow a finding of a contravention of the
Act,
despite that the target group is still not "likely" to be exposed to hatred or contempt. I do not believe this is what is intended by the
Act.

[
123
]  For those reasons, I believe the test applied in
CJC
is not applicable to s. 2 of the
Act.

[
124
]  Beyond the requirements of the specific statute, however, a high degree of flexibility will be required in the application of any test in order to allow for a broad contextual assessment in each case. The tests should be viewed as providing an analytical framework rather than a template to be mechanically applied in every case. In order for such a framework to be viable, it must permit a contextual consideration of both the effect and the content of the message.

[
125
]  Accordingly, in my opinion,
the test set out in
Abrams
as modified to reflect the
Act
's requirements would be one such standard which may be applied in the context of s. 2(1)(b). Such a test might enquire:

Does the communication itself express hatred or contempt of a person or group on a basis of one or more of the listed grounds? Would a reasonable person, informed about the context, understand the message as expressing hatred or contempt?

Assessed in its context, is the likely effect of the communication to make it more acceptable to others to manifest hatred or contempt against the person or group concerned? Would a reasonable person consider it more likely than not to expose members of the target group to hatred and contempt?

The Unitary Test

[
126
]
Section 13
of the
Canadian Human Rights Act
provides that it is a discriminatory practice for a person or a group of persons to communicate telephonically in "any matter that is likely to expose a person or persons to hatred or contempt". The Federal Tribunal applies a unitary test. Drawing from the Tribunals' decisions and the Supreme Court of Canada's
decision in
Taylor
,
LEAF suggests the following is an articulation of the test applied in the context of s. 13(1) of the Federal legislation:

Is the matter in the message more likely than not to spark a positive reaction among some of the listeners to it, which will likely manifest itself in hatred (extreme ill will; finding no redeeming qualities) or contempt (looked down upon, despised) towards the targets of the messages.

[
127
]  As noted above, a flexible approach to determining a breach under s. 2(1) is necessary. However, the question, in the context of s. 2 of the
Act,
is not whether the listener has been persuaded, but rather whether the target group is more likely to be exposed to hatred and contempt as a result of the representation. Accordingly, the unitary test, as stated above, is inapplicable to s. 2(1)(b) of the
Act.

(IV)  THE FACTORS TO CONSIDER

[
128
]  Tribunals have considered a number of factors in relation to the communication, the target group and the method of publication, in order to determine whether the respective test has been satisfied. These include:

(i)       content of the communication:
Kane, CJC, Abrams;

(ii)       tone of the communication:
CJC, Abrams;

(iii)      the image conveyed, including whether the use of quotations or reference sources gives the message more credibility:
Nealy;

(iv)      vulnerability of the target group:
Nealy, CJC, Abrams;

(v)       the degree to which the expression reinforces existing stereotypes:
Kane, Abrams, Nealy;

(vi)      the circumstances surrounding the message, including whether the messages appeal to well-publicized issues:
Nealy;

(vii)     the medium used to convey the message:
Nealy, CJC, Abrams;

(viii)    circulation of the publication:
CJC, Abrams, Nealy;

(ix)      credibility to be accorded to the communication:
Abrams, Nealy;
and

(x)       the context of publication, for example whether it is part of a debate or whether it is presented as news or as a purportedly authoritative analysis:
CJC, Abrams.

[
129
]  Although the above list may serve as some guidance to human rights tribunals, it is not exhaustive and the full context of each case will have to be considered to determine whether s. 2(1)(b) of the
Act
has been contravened.

(c)  Opinion

[
130
]  The definitions of "contempt" and "hatred", for the purposes of human rights legislation, have been settled by a majority of
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Taylor
.
Those definitions dictate that different considerations apply to each of those terms. The definition of "likely to expose" should focus on the impact of the communication on the target group, specifically, whether the communication makes it more likely than not that the target group will be exposed to hatred and contempt. Any test applied to determine whether a representation "is likely to expose a person or class of persons to hatred or contempt" must be highly contextual and responsive to the legislation. Further, such a test should be viewed as an analytical framework rather than as a template. In applying such a framework, the Panel should draw from the various factors and considerations used in other cases, including, but not limited to:

”¢    the message – content, tone, images conveyed, reinforcement of stereotypes, surround circumstances;

”¢    the medium – credibility, circulation, context of the publication; and

”¢    the audience -– vulnerability of target group.
